title: If viewers leave in three seconds, stop writing introductions
markdown:
# If viewers leave in three seconds, stop writing introductions

At 8:14 p.m., a creator exports a 27-second video about a useful idea, posts it, and watches the retention line fall off a cliff before the first sentence has finished. The edit is clean. The advice is sound. None of that matters if the opening gives a thumb a reason to keep moving.

That is the problem worth fixing first. A hook is not a dramatic voiceover or a pile of caps-lock promises. It is the first beat that tells a stranger, "this is about the problem I have," and makes staying feel cheaper than swiping.

## Start with the moment the viewer recognizes

Most weak openings begin with the creator's context: "In this video, I want to talk about..." The viewer has not agreed to care yet. Put them in the middle of a familiar failure instead.

If you teach freelancers, open on the client who says they need a quote "today" and then vanishes for two weeks. If you teach cooking, open on the pan that looks done on top and stays raw in the middle. If you make fitness videos, use the exact point in a workout when a beginner wonders whether the exercise is doing anything at all.

The detail does two jobs. It selects the right person, and it proves that the video has a destination. "Your first five client calls are probably going wrong before you mention price" is stronger than "Five tips for better sales calls" because the first line contains a live problem. The viewer can test it against their own day.

## Put the payoff close enough to touch

Curiosity can carry a few seconds, but vague curiosity wears out fast. Give the viewer a clear promise early: a mistake they can spot, a choice they can make, or a result they can try for themselves.

Compare these openings:

- "You need to hear this about content."
- "Your tutorial loses people when the first sentence explains the topic instead of showing the mistake."

The second one is narrower. Good. A short video does not need to win everyone. It needs to keep the person who has that problem long enough to deliver the fix.

There is a useful test here: could someone repeat the opening in plain language after hearing it once? If the answer is "it was about being more intentional," the line is too foggy. If they can say, "it showed why my first sentence is losing viewers," you have something to work with.

## Make the opening sound like the video that follows

A hook can earn a pause and still fail the video. This happens when the first line makes a huge promise, then the next 20 seconds become generic advice. The viewer did not get tricked by an algorithm. They got tricked by the gap between the opening and the substance.

Write the first line after you know the useful point of the video. Then check the join between the two. If the hook says "the reason your recipe videos look flat," the next shot should show a flat-looking plate or name the lighting choice that causes it. Do not make viewers wait through a greeting, a bio, or a throat-clearing setup.

This also makes testing less painful. When one opening performs poorly, you can replace the opening while leaving the actual lesson intact. You are testing the doorway, not rebuilding the house.

## Draft several hooks before you pick one

The first hook that arrives is usually an explanation, because explanations are how creators think. The viewer needs an entry point, not your notes.

Take one video idea and make five starts with different angles. Use a specific mistake. Use a recognizable scene. State a surprising constraint. Put the result before the method. Ask a question only if the question has teeth.

For a video about unresponsive prospects, a batch might look like this:

- "If a prospect says 'circle back next month,' do not send another 'just checking in' email."
- "The follow-up that gets ignored usually starts with the same five words."
- "A client who goes quiet after your proposal is not always saying no."
- "Before you lower your rate, read the last sentence of your proposal."
- "You can lose a warm lead by making the next step too easy to postpone."

They are not interchangeable. Each makes a different promise. Read them aloud, then choose the one that most honestly leads into the footage you already have.

If you want help generating and pressure-testing those alternatives, [Hook Lab](https://capafy.ai/agent/8123079349?ct=hooklab_blog) is built for that narrow job: turning a video idea into openings that give the right viewer a reason to stop.

The goal is not to sound louder. It is to stop wasting the first three seconds on a preamble. Put the viewer's problem on screen, make one honest promise, and get to the proof before their thumb does.
